cue: Things that move glow. The sharp cross jumps to them, looks them over, and then leaves that place alone for a few seconds.

SIDE_GREEN.note: the side eyes’ one green class as a dim green; the tint is invented

UV_GREEN.note: green as green and ultraviolet as blue, red their mean; receptor fits in research/methods

UV_GREEN_RED.note: the red-filtered class as red, green as green, ultraviolet as blue; receptor fits in research/methods

rows: Six of a jumping spider’s eyes watch for movement all around it, and two large front eyes swing toward whatever they report to look closely. This view draws all eight as one picture.

The six side eyes see in green only, and with little detail: under a hundredth of yours at the back and about a fiftieth in front. They answer only to movement, so here the surround is a dim green and whatever moves in it glows.
The front side eyes pick out the jointed, rhythmic movement of living things, and the rear side eyes answer to anything that moves. In front, this view makes living movement glow brighter.

Each large front eye sees a narrow upright strip about 2 degrees wide and 21 high, bent in the middle, and the two strips cross like an X. In Phidippus they see about a sixteenth of the detail you do, and in Portia about a fifth.

The front eyes jump to a new target in about a tenth of a second and follow it if it moves. While they look, they sweep side to side across it and slowly twist back and forth, and this view does the same.

Once the front eyes lock on, the side eyes ignore that spot and watch elsewhere, and their interest in it returns over about five seconds. Here the glow fades from a place just looked at and comes back as slowly.

Most jumping spiders, Phidippus among them, see ultraviolet and green. Habronattus also sees red, in a small patch at the centre of each front eye, and this view adds red there when it knows the genus.

At night a resting jumping spider’s retinas twitch in bouts, much like the eye movements of a person dreaming. When the phone lies still in the dark, this view twitches its cross in bouts, closer together than a spider’s.
No one knows how a jumping spider joins what its eyes report. Drawing the front eyes’ cross inside the side eyes’ surround, as one picture, is the app’s own choice.
This view treats movement that holds together over a small patch and swings back and forth, as walking legs do, as the movement of something alive. That test is the app’s own approximation.

A phone camera records almost no ultraviolet light, so the ultraviolet in this view is a guess made from bluish and bright surfaces. Inside the cross the spider’s green shows as green and the guessed ultraviolet as blue, with red for their mix.
A jumping spider senses low sounds in the air through hairs on its legs. The picture leaves this out.
